requirements.requirement: On node1, only root and opsadmin can schedule cron jobs (cron.allow enforcement)
requirements.summary: Executor discovered busybox crond has no allow/deny mechanism, installed cronie (which honors /etc/cron.allow), created opsadmin, wrote /etc/cron.allow containing only root and opsadmin, removed /etc/cron.deny, and enabled the cronie crond service. Directly verified root and opsadmin can write crontabs while a disposable testuser is rejected with 'not allowed to use this program (crontab)'. This enforcement was re-verified with a fresh verifyuser after a full node restart, confirming durability.

requirements.requirement: Existing cron functionality (root's system periodic crontab) is preserved and test artifacts are cleaned up
requirements.summary: Root's original run-parts periodic crontab (15min/hourly/daily/weekly/monthly) was captured, temporarily overwritten during testing, then restored verbatim and confirmed present both immediately after and after the restart. Test users (testuser, verifyuser) and opsadmin's throwaway test crontab entry were removed and confirmed absent.

requirements.requirement: Provider-wide node-restart evidence protocol executed on node1 with healthy baseline, restart, changed boot identity, and recovered state
requirements.summary: Pre-restart boot_id (961c70eb...) and healthy baseline (crond running, cron.allow correct, root crontab intact) were captured, a backgrounded /sbin/reboot was issued and acknowledged, the connection dropped during the outage (several failed polls), and a new boot_id (ae8d48cd...) was observed after polling resumed, matching the independent global before/after-executor boot-identity snapshots. Post-restart checks confirmed cronie's crond service running, cron.allow intact, root's crontab intact, and enforcement still denying a fresh test user.

overall_summary: The task (restricting cron scheduling on node1 to root and opsadmin) is fully and directly satisfied: busybox crond's lack of allow/deny support was correctly diagnosed and replaced with cronie, /etc/cron.allow was set to exactly root and opsadmin, enforcement was proven against a disposable third user, and root's pre-existing periodic crontab was preserved. The independently required node-restart evidence protocol was also completed correctly with a clear pre/post boot-identity transition and full recovery of cron configuration, service, and crontab state, corroborated by the fixed lifecycle snapshots. Hygiene is good; the only notable deviations are an intentional removal of the package-shipped /etc/cron.deny (flagged by apk verify but functionally harmless) and two small leftover log files in /tmp.
limitations: The after_prepare snapshot is an alias of before_prepare (prepare was disabled), so preparer-vs-executor state could only be assessed against the initial baseline rather than a distinct prepared state.

Removal of /etc/cron.deny caused a package-manager verification flag (X) in the after-executor package-health snapshot; this is a minor, intentional deviation from pristine package state rather than a functional defect.

Captured command outputs are truncated for long directory/service listings, but the evidence relevant to the material outcomes (cron.allow content, crontab contents, service status, boot_id) is complete and directly observed.

operational_hygiene.summary: All state-changing commands trace clearly to the task: installing cronie, creating opsadmin, writing cron.allow, enabling the crond service, and the mandatory restart cycle. Disposable test users (testuser, verifyuser) and test crontab entries were created solely to prove allow/deny enforcement and were fully removed afterward (cmd-c713768062154d85, cmd-ff665fd4d1a64eea, cmd-0ed7c583ff064deb, cmd-b1a621c326a24409), leaving no residue. One minor deviation: removing /etc/cron.deny (part of cmd-bf7d86bf4fe44735) caused the package-health check to flag 'X etc/cron.deny' as missing relative to the cronie package's shipped file in the after-executor snapshot — a low-risk, intentional change (cron.allow alone is sufficient and avoids conflicting allow/deny semantics) but it does technically diverge from the pristine package-manager state. Two harmless leftover log files (/tmp/apk-install.log, /tmp/reboot.log) remain in /tmp, a bounded and low-risk residue from routine install/reboot logging.
